# Regional Research Guides

Moved from SKILL.md (Phase 3 "Research by Region" and Phase 6 NC-specific strategies). Read the relevant section before searching a specific region.

### Research by Region

#### Southeastern NC (Brunswick, Columbus, Bladen, New Hanover)

**Record availability timeline:**
- **1764**: Brunswick County formed from New Hanover and Bladen
- **Pre-1764**: Records in New Hanover and Bladen counties
- **Colonial era (1660s-1776)**: NC colonial records, land patents, quit rents, vestry records
- **1790+**: Federal census (NC lost 1790 returns — use tax lists as substitute)
- **1868+**: NC vital registration becomes spotty; not reliable until ~1913
- **Church records**: Often pre-date civil records significantly

**Research strategy for Brunswick County:**
1. Start with Ancestry tree hints and attached records
2. Federal census records (1800-1940) for household composition
3. NC marriage bonds (often available from 1700s)
4. Land and deed records (crucial for placing families geographically)
5. Probate/will records (name all heirs)
6. Church records (Baptist and Methodist most common in the area)
7. Cemetery records (Find A Grave, local cemetery transcriptions)
8. NC State Archives for military and colonial records
9. DigitalNC for newspaper mentions and local histories

**Local knowledge — Shallotte/Brunswick area:**
- Many families were farmers, fishermen, and naval stores workers (turpentine/tar)
- The Intracoastal Waterway and barrier islands shaped settlement patterns
- Hurricane histories affected records — some courthouses lost records to storms
- Vereen, Hewett, and Gore are quintessential lower Brunswick County names
- Churches (especially Shallotte Baptist, various Methodist churches) kept records

#### Central NC (Johnston, Chatham, Harnett)

**Key sources:**
- Johnston County courthouse records (Smithfield)
- Chatham County courthouse records (Pittsboro)
- Harnett County courthouse records (Lillington)
- Heritage of Johnston County (published county history)
- Heritage of Chatham County (published county history)

**Research strategy:**
- These counties were agricultural (tobacco, cotton)
- Many families moved between these adjacent counties
- Check for the same family in multiple county records
- Chatham County Quaker records may apply for some lines

#### Horry County, South Carolina

**Key sources:**
- Horry County courthouse (Conway, SC)
- SC Department of Archives and History (scdah.sc.gov)
- Independent Republic Quarterly (Horry County historical journal)
- FamilySearch SC collections

**Important context:**
- Brunswick County, NC and Horry County, SC share a border
- Many families (especially Vereen) spanned both sides
- The Little River area is essentially one community divided by a state line
- Check BOTH states for any family near the NC/SC border

#### Nebraska (Jefferson & Gage Counties)

**Key sources:**
- Nebraska State Historical Society (nebraskahistory.org)
- FamilySearch NE collections
- Federal census 1860-1940
- NE county marriage records
- Homestead records (General Land Office — glorecords.blm.gov)
- Fairbury and Beatrice newspaper archives

**Important context:**
- The Moritz family connection to Nebraska suggests German immigration
- Many German and Czech immigrants settled southeastern Nebraska in the 1860s-1880s
- Homestead Act records are critical — they document when families arrived and where they settled
- Check for German-language church records (Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic)

#### Southwestern Virginia / Southern WV (Tazewell, Mercer Counties)

**Key sources:**
- Library of Virginia (lva.virginia.gov) — extensive digitized records
- VA Land Office patents and grants
- WV Division of Culture and History (wvculture.org)
- Tazewell County Historical Society
- Federal census for VA and WV
- Clear Fork and Rock district records

**Important context:**
- Tazewell County is Appalachian — different record-keeping culture than coastal NC
- The Livingston family likely connects to Scots-Irish settlement patterns
- West Virginia separated from Virginia in 1863 — check both for Civil War era
- Coal mining and railroad records may be relevant for early 1900s

#### Serbia / Vojvodina (Ratkovo, Odžaci)

**Key sources:**
- Serbian Archives (arhivvojvodine.org.rs) — Archives of Vojvodina
- FamilySearch has limited Serbian records
- Ratkovo is a small village in the Odžaci municipality
- Church records (Orthodox, Catholic, or Protestant depending on ethnicity)
- Matične knjige (vital records registers)

**Important context:**
- Vojvodina was part of Austria-Hungary until 1918
- Records may be in Serbian, Hungarian, or German depending on era
- The Rocchetti surname is Italian in origin — possibly Italian immigrants to Vojvodina (there were Italian communities in the Habsburg Empire)
- Check both Serbian AND Austro-Hungarian archives
- Immigration records (Ellis Island, Castle Garden) for arrival in the US

#### England (Devon, Somerset, Cheshire)

**Key sources:**
- FamilySearch English parish registers (extensive and mostly free)
- FindMyPast (findmypast.com) — British records specialist
- The National Archives (nationalarchives.gov.uk)
- Devon Heritage Centre (devon.gov.uk)
- Somerset Heritage Centre
- Cheshire Archives

**Important context:**
- Oakford, Devon connections suggest West Country English origin
- St. Decumans Parish, Somerset is near Watchet on the Bristol Channel
- These are colonial-era connections — families likely came to the Carolinas in the 1600s-1700s
- Check colonial ship passenger lists and early NC colonial records
- The Parrish surname connects to St. Decumans — parish records may go back to the 1500s

## Phase 6: NC-Specific Research Strategies

### Colonial & Revolutionary Era (pre-1790)

For the oldest branches (Parrish, Gore, early Brunswick families):
- NC Colonial Records (digitized at docsouth.unc.edu)
- NC Land Grant Files (nclandgrants.com)
- Revolutionary War pension applications (fold3.com or Ancestry)
- Tax lists as census substitutes (NC lost most 1790 census returns)
- Vestry records (Anglican/Episcopal church governance records — listed residents)

### Antebellum Period (1790-1860)

- Federal census every 10 years
- Slave schedules (1850, 1860) — list enslaver and number of enslaved people by age/sex
- Agricultural census schedules — farm size, crops, livestock
- NC marriage bonds (often from county formation onward)
- Court minutes and deed books

### Civil War Era (1861-1865)

**NC sent more troops than any Confederate state.** For Brunswick County families:
- NC Troops, 1861-1865 (published roster — searchable at ncpedia.org)
- Confederate muster rolls (Fold3.com, NC State Archives)
- Union records (if applicable — some NC coastal families were Unionist)
- Pension records (NC Confederate pensions from 1885+)
- Brunswick County likely sent men to regiments organized in Wilmington area

### Reconstruction & Jim Crow Era (1865-1920)

- Freedmen's Bureau records (if applicable)
- First census with formerly enslaved people named (1870)
- NC vital registration begins sporadically (reliable from ~1913)
- Church records become more important in the gap

### The "Brick Wall" Strategy for Southeastern NC

Common brick walls and how to break through:

| Wall | Strategy |
|---|---|
| No birth certificates before 1913 | Use census, church records, family Bible records |
| Lost courthouse records (fires, hurricanes) | NC State Archives microfilm, neighboring county records |
| Common surname (Gore, Martin, Johnson) | Use land records to place family geographically, then cross-reference |
| Pre-1850 census (only head of household) | Tax lists, deed witnesses, court records fill in names |
| Female ancestors "disappear" | Marriage bonds name fathers; wills name daughters |
| Family moved between counties | Check ALL adjacent counties (Columbus, Bladen, New Hanover, Horry SC) |
